design_problem.problem_statement: A hospital delivery robot (Aethon TUG) wakes up from a power failure inside a large hospital with a known floor plan. It has a 2D LIDAR and wheel encoders. It does NOT know its starting position. Task: solve this same localization problem three times, using three fundamentally different algorithms — Histogram Filter, EKF, and Particle Filter — and compare what breaks in each approach as the environment complexity increases.
design_problem.real_world_context: Aethon TUG autonomous hospital robot is deployed in over 140 hospitals worldwide. After a power failure, the robot must re-localize without human intervention to resume medicine and supply delivery. Global localization after power loss is a real operational requirement.

failure_modes.naive_approach: Discretize the hospital floor plan into a 1 cm grid. Assign equal probability to every grid cell. Update the distribution after each LIDAR scan. Use the highest-probability cell as the position estimate.
critical_questions: A hospital floor plan is 200 m × 100 m. At 1 cm resolution, how many cells are needed?
How do you update 2 billion cells at 10 Hz?
What happens to the discrete probability distribution when the robot enters a long, uniform corridor where many cells look identical?
Is the belief distribution unimodal (single position) or multimodal (multiple possible positions)?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: A 200 × 100 m hospital at 1 cm resolution requires 200,000,000 cells. Updating each cell at 10 Hz requires 2 × 10⁹ operations per second — impossible on embedded hardware. Additionally, in a symmetric hospital corridor, many grid cells will have identical observation probabilities, creating a multimodal distribution (robot could be at any of several identical-looking locations).
failure_modes.failure_consequence: The histogram filter requires 60 GB RAM and cannot run in real time. Even at degraded 10 cm resolution, the robot cannot distinguish its location in a long uniform corridor — it correctly identifies 'a corridor' but not 'which of the 12 identical corridors'.
failure_modes.resolving_concept_name_ar: تحديد مكان ماركوف ومرشح الرسم البياني
failure_modes.scientific_principle: Histogram filter (Discrete Bayes Filter): bel(x_t) implemented as a probability table over discrete cells. Algorithm: (1) Predict: redistribute probability across neighbors according to motion model; (2) Update: multiply each cell by p(z|x_cell); (3) Normalize. The Markov assumption: p(x_t | x_{0:t-1}, z_{0:t}, u_{0:t}) = p(x_t | x_{t-1}, z_t, u_t) — state encodes all relevant history. Strength: handles multimodal distributions (global localization). Weakness: O(N) memory and computation where N = number of grid cells.

citation.location: Chapter 4: Nonparametric Filters, Section 4.1, Pages 94–101 — Histogram Filter algorithm

failure_modes.comparative_notes: The histogram filter is the FIRST algorithm — it is intuitive and handles global uncertainty. Its failure (computation cost, resolution limit) motivates the EKF in F-006-02.

failure_modes.naive_approach: The hospital layout has known wall positions. Represent the robot's position as a Gaussian distribution N(μ, Σ) — just a mean position and a covariance ellipse. Update it when LIDAR scans arrive.
critical_questions: The LIDAR observation model z = h(x) involves arctan() and sqrt() — these are nonlinear functions. What does that do to a Gaussian input?
The motion model x_next = f(x, u) also involves sin() and cos() — nonlinear. How do you propagate a Gaussian through a nonlinear function?
When the robot enters a long corridor and could be at multiple positions, can a single Gaussian represent this?
What is the Jacobian, and what does linearizing the motion model mean?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: The standard Kalman Filter requires linear dynamics. The robot's motion model (sin, cos) and observation model (range/bearing) are both nonlinear. Passing a Gaussian through a nonlinear function produces a non-Gaussian result. Pretending the output is still Gaussian introduces linearization error. Additionally, a Gaussian cannot represent multimodal uncertainty (two possible positions in a symmetric corridor).
failure_modes.failure_consequence: In a corridor junction, the robot is equally likely to be at two positions (symmetric junction). The EKF forces a single Gaussian — it places the mean between the two positions, in an empty hallway. The robot executes a motion based on a position estimate that is 3 m from any wall, causing immediate collision.
failure_modes.resolving_concept_name: Extended Kalman Filter for Robot Localization

citation.location: Chapter 3: Gaussian Filters, Section 3.3, Pages 53–73 — EKF derivation, Jacobian computation, failure modes

failure_modes.naive_approach: Wrap the EKF in a Gaussian mixture to handle multimodal beliefs. Use 10 Gaussians to track 10 possible positions simultaneously.
critical_questions: After each LIDAR update, how do the 10 Gaussians get reweighted?
When 9 of the 10 positions are ruled out and only 1 remains, how does the mixture collapse?
What if the true position is NOT near any of the initial 10 Gaussians?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: Gaussian mixtures require pre-specifying the number of modes (10), but in global localization the number of possible positions is unknown. If the true position falls between two initial Gaussians, both will drift away — the mixture fails to track the true state. Additionally, managing Gaussian component weights, births, and deaths is algorithmically complex.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: In a hospital with 47 rooms that all look identical in LIDAR, the robot initializes 10 Gaussians but the true position is in room 23 — not near any of the 10 initial guesses. All Gaussians drift to wrong positions. The robot delivers medication to the wrong room.
failure_modes.resolving_concept_name: Particle Filters and Monte Carlo Localization
failure_modes.scientific_principle:
Particle Filter (Sequential Monte Carlo): represent bel(x) as a set of N weighted particles {<x^[i], w^[i]>}_{i=1:N}. Algorithm:
  1. Predict: sample x_t^[i] ~ p(x_t | u_t, x_{t-1}^[i])  [apply noisy motion to each particle]
  2. Weight:  w^[i] = p(z_t | x_t^[i])                   [score each particle by observation likelihood]
  3. Resample: draw N particles with replacement, weighted by w^[i] [eliminate bad particles]
MCL exploits: particles automatically concentrate where the probability is high. For global localization, start with N=10,000 particles uniformly covering the floor plan. Strength: nonparametric (any distribution shape), handles multimodal uncertainty. Weakness: particle deprivation when N is too small; computationally O(N) per step.

citation.location: Chapter 4: Nonparametric Filters, Section 4.3, Pages 96–122 — Particle Filter, MCL algorithm, convergence

real_world_example.description: The Aethon TUG hospital robot uses a particle filter-based localization system (AMCL) implemented in ROS. It initializes with a uniform distribution over the entire floor plan and typically converges to the correct location within 3–5 meters of travel.

failure_modes.naive_approach: Once MCL converges (particles concentrate around one position), keep running with 10,000 particles to maintain accuracy.
critical_questions: Once the robot knows where it is (tracking mode), do we still need 10,000 particles?
How does the Gaussian tracking mode (EKF) compare to the particle filter tracking mode?
Can we switch between EKF (efficient tracking) and MCL (global localization) based on the current belief entropy?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: Running 10,000 particles in tracking mode wastes computation — once the belief is unimodal and narrow, a single Gaussian requires only 6 numbers vs 10,000 × 3 numbers = 30,000. The GaussianFilter approach (EKF) is far more efficient for tracking. The insight: EKF and particle filter complement each other — particle filter for global localization, EKF for tracking once converged.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: The hospital robot uses 10,000 particles at all times. The full compute budget is consumed by localization, leaving no CPU for path planning. The robot freezes every 2 seconds while the particle filter update completes.
failure_modes.scientific_principle:
Gaussian localization assumes the belief is unimodal and approximately Gaussian — valid for tracking mode after successful global localization. EKF-localization: state x = [x, y, θ], landmark positions known. Update: for each observed landmark l at relative bearing α:
  innovation: z̃ = z_observed − h(x̂, l)
  gain: K = P·H^T·(H·P·H^T + R)^{-1}
  update: x̂ = x̂ + K·z̃; P = (I − K·H)·P
EKF localization is O(n) per landmark observation (vs O(N) for particle filter) and is exact for linear-Gaussian systems.
